source.title: Memorization in Self-Supervised Learning Improves Downstream Generalization
source.authors: Wen-Hao Wang; Muhammad Ahmad Kaleem; Adam Dziedzic; Michael Backes; Nicolas Papernot; Franziska Boenisch

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present, including appendices; no apparent cutoff or garbling affects the extracted results.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures SSL memorization using representation alignment and tests its relationship to downstream generalization by removing memorized training examples or limiting alignment. This is a different method and setting from the listed versions.
record.gate_note: The study reports that removing highly memorized SSL pretraining examples harms downstream performance more than removing random examples. These results concern unlabeled SSL encoders and downstream tasks, so they do not test the listed supervised-learning versions. The paper also reports memorization and accuracy associations, but those correlations alone do not establish the listed versions.
record.test_reason: The study measures memorization through changes in SSL representation alignment and evaluates downstream performance. V8 instead defines memorized examples through their influence on predicting their own labels. The paper explicitly distinguishes these constructs; none of its experiments tests V1–V8.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that SSL encoders memorize especially atypical examples and that memorization improves downstream generalization, including across distributions and beyond classification. This is their interpretation of representation-based memorization, not a demonstrated result about V8's label-based criterion.
record.recipe_differences: Self-supervised encoder training and representation-alignment memorization; evaluates transfer-task performance rather than supervised natural-label test error or random-label fitting.
record.method_sensitivity: Downstream dataset and task, number of memorized examples removed, and regularization strength limiting alignment affect reported downstream outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: Removing examples ranked highest by SSLMem harms downstream performance more than removing equal numbers of random examples. For example, removing 20k ImageNet examples gives ImageNet probing accuracy 58.90% versus 62.88% after random removal, and depth RMSE 0.311 versus 0.302.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Examples whose inclusion most improves SSL representation alignment can contribute disproportionately to downstream classification, segmentation, and depth performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Training on highly SSLMem-ranked subsets can retain or numerically improve performance: retaining 24k gives CIFAR10 accuracy 64.4% versus 63.3% with 25k; retaining 22k gives CIFAR100 accuracy 61.8% versus 61.1%. These comparisons lack equal-size random-subset controls.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SSLMem ranking can select smaller SSL training subsets that retain downstream linear-probe performance in some settings.

record.problems: The authors describe their SSLMem estimate as an approximation to the leave-one-out definition; the main removal figures do not provide exact plotted values in the supplied text. The tabular results compare memorized-example removal with random-example removal, but do not establish the listed supervised-learning claims.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 3 reports removal counts 1k, 2k, 4k, and 8k for CIFAR100 and STL10 downstream evaluations, but provides figure-only values in the supplied text. These repetitive figure-only rows were omitted; the text states the qualitative direction for all downstream tasks. Table 14 has been represented for each displayed dataset and removal count; the source table formatting is flattened and some percent signs are absent.

untested.parts: No comparison of fitting fixed random labels and generalizing on natural labels under the same recipe.
No width sweep establishing zero training error and subsequent test-error behavior. Table 15's architecture comparison does not establish this.
No convolutional-versus-fully-connected comparison or isolation of local connectivity.
No controlled batch-size comparison under a fixed epoch budget.
No dropout intervention or dropout–augmentation–weight-decay comparison.
No magnitude-aware sharpness measurement or ranking of generalization gaps against norm and margin measures.

No removal experiment selecting examples by their influence on predicting their own labels. The supervised experiments compare memorization scores and rankings, without testing the required removal effect.

record.verdict_notes: The record's tests/T2 classification conflicts with its own gate note and should be corrected. States are cannot_determine relative to the listed versions; this does not deny the reported SSL removal effects. Appendix B.3 and Table 12 report only partial overlap between representation-based and supervised memorization rankings, reinforcing that the criteria are not interchangeable. No missing results bear directly on V1–V8.

versions.untested_parts: Does not train the listed architectures on fixed random labels and natural labels or compare held-out accuracy.
Does not sweep one-hidden-layer ReLU width past the interpolation threshold.
Does not compare convolutional and fully connected networks on image classification.
Does not compare adaptive optimizers with SGD on the listed benchmarks.
Does not test large-batch generalization under fixed epoch budgets.
Does not test dropout or its interaction with data augmentation and weight decay.
Does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness or compare it with norm- or margin-based measures.

Uses SSL representation alignment to identify memorized examples, not the version’s label-based influence criterion; tests downstream performance after removing SSL pretraining examples, not the specified supervised setting.
